name: AI Case Law: The Precedents Behind the Defenses
blurb: The older decisions AI defendants are actually relying on. Every current AI copyright, scraping and defamation case is argued out of a small set of precedents decided long before generative models existed: Sony on substantial non-infringing use, Campbell and Google Books on transformative purpose, Van Buren and hiQ on scraping, Zeran on Section 230. Each profile states what the case held, why AI defendants cite it, and where the analogy is weakest, with a link to the opinion itself.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Selling a technology that can be used to infringe is not itself contributory infringement when the technology is capable of substantial non-infringing uses. Home recording of broadcast television for later viewing was held to be fair use.
cases.case_name: Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A commercial parody can be fair use. The Court made transformative purpose the centre of the first fair use factor and rejected the idea that commercial use is presumptively unfair.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Facts are not copyrightable, however much labour went into collecting them. Only original selection, coordination and arrangement can be protected, and effort alone earns nothing.
cases.case_name: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Copying a program in full in order to study it is fair use when that copying is the only way to reach the unprotected functional elements inside and there is a legitimate reason to reach them.
cases.case_name: Sega Enterprises Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: A search engine that copied photographs and displayed them as thumbnails made fair use, because the thumbnails served an indexing function rather than the original artistic one.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Image search thumbnails were fair use, and the court adopted a server test under which a site that merely frames an image hosted elsewhere does not display it for copyright purposes.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: Digitising a library of books to enable full-text search and access for print-disabled readers was fair use, and the search function was squarely transformative.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: Scanning millions of books without permission and showing snippets in response to searches was fair use. The court treated the purpose as providing information about the books rather than substituting for them.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Copying roughly 11,500 lines of a software interface to let developers reuse what they already knew was fair use. The Court assumed copyrightability and decided the case on fair use instead.
cases.case_name: Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Distributing a tool with the object of promoting its use to infringe, shown by clear expression or affirmative steps, creates liability for the resulting infringement.
cases.case_name: Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: The section 512(c) safe harbour requires knowledge of specific infringing material, not a general awareness that infringement occurs on a service.
cases.case_name: Viacom International, Inc. v. YouTube, Inc.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: Section 230 bars treating an interactive computer service as the publisher of information provided by another, and notice of the content does not remove that protection.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Scraping data that a website makes publicly available without any login does not amount to access without authorisation under the CFAA.
cases.case_name: hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Exceeding authorised access under the CFAA means obtaining information from areas of a computer that are off limits, not using information you were entitled to obtain for a purpose the owner would dislike.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The first fair use factor asks whether the challenged use shares the same purpose as the original, especially where both are licensed into the same market. Adding new meaning or message is not by itself enough.
cases.case_name: Andy Warhol Foundation for Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith
